processing: Made by the Tieguanyin method rather than the lighter local baozhong style, with fuller oxidation and repeated rolling; a charcoal-roasted version is a local speciality.
harvest_season: Little is documented about picking dates here; as with other northern Taiwanese oolongs, spring and winter lots are generally the ones most sought after.
appearance_dry: Dark brown rolled leaf with an oily sheen.
appearance_liquor: Amber to reddish gold, deeper in charcoal-roasted lots.
appearance_wet: Thick, soft leaves that open slowly and show browned edges, as is usual for a roasted rolled oolong.
taste_profile: A full, rounded body with a light fruity acidity; the charcoal-roasted version adds warmth and toastiness.

brewing.notes: Typical gongfu settings for a roasted rolled oolong. Use near-boiling water and give the rolled leaf time to open.

vintage_note: Sold as a regional oolong from local farmers and the farmers' association, by harvest season where the seller states it. Roasted oolongs of this kind are normally drunk within a year or two of roasting, though they keep better than green-style oolongs if sealed; no established market for aged Shimen lots is documented.
description:
Shimen sits at the far northern tip of Taiwan, and its best-known tea is a local Tieguanyin. It is a useful reminder that the name is both a cultivar and a way of making tea: here the method seems to matter more than the plant.

Local accounts say growers had long made baozhong from Yingzhi Hongxin bushes, whose sturdy stems and thick, soft leaves turned out better suited to the Tieguanyin method. The result is dark and rolled, and a charcoal-roasted version has become a favourite with local buyers.

In the cup, expect a rounded, full body with a gentle fruity sourness rather than the orchid perfume of modern Anxi green-style Tieguanyin. As with other roasted oolongs, near-boiling water suits it and short first steeps keep the roast from dominating.

It is a small regional tea, mostly sold close to home. Ask the seller about the season and the roast level, since a heavily charcoal-roasted lot and a lighter one taste quite different. If you know Muzha Tieguanyin from Taipei, it makes the natural comparison.
history:
Shimen's tea was traditionally baozhong. Reports date the shift to the Tieguanyin method to around the 1980s, when the local farmers' association and Taiwan's tea research station guided growers towards it; that date rests on local accounts and is not firmly documented.

By 2004 a national agriculture publication was naming Shimen Tieguanyin among the township's specialities and noting the appeal of the charcoal-roasted version.
